Rand Paul is currently my favorite candidate running for president. However, I would like to see his rebuttal to the charge that his 14.5% tax proposal for "business activity" is a value added tax. Note: I'm biased; I'm a Libertarian and I like Rand.

I'll address the economic parts of his platform that I take issue with from his website

Spending and Debt

Rand supports a Balanced Budget Amendment to the constitution, which is pretty much pure idiocy. During recessions the government is supposed to act as the buyer/employer of last resort and stop aggregate demand from falling dramatically by deficit spending, such as with the ARRA. Too much or too little debt can be harmful to an economies growth, but to mandate a balanced budget at all times, which is de facto austerity during recessions, won't work too well.

Taxes

Disregarding that capital income taxes and corporate taxes are the worst kind of taxes, (they're horribly distortionary, discourage work, cause capital flight and are incredibly prone to tax evasion) Rand's plan isn't too bad. Maybe there could be 1 or 2 more tax brackets for people making above $200K or $500K to make it more progressive.

Audit the Fed

This one is pure populism. The Fed is audited by the GAO, OIG and another private firm. The real goal of this bill is to compromise the Fed's independence by allowing the Comptroller to call an audit at any time.

Immigration

The economic effects of immigration are almost purely beneficial. What he's espousing in't necessarily bad policy; it's just not optimal. The ideal would be very weak immigration controls.

Social Security

In general Social Security could be such a better system. Superannuation funds like in Australia would be a great alternative. It certainly has its issues but it manages to create a low cost, high return, sustainable retirement system.

I'm not sure I know what libertarianism means anymore. Back in the day, it implied a lack of government oversight and control, with a judiciary meting out justice when peoples rights were violated by other individuals or entities.

This all made perfect sense when reading Ayn Rand novels. Everything always worked better when a libertarian approach was used.

The advantage of Ayn Rand libertarianism is that just about anyone can understand the philosophy of it, and on the surface it seems to make perfect sense.

One problem with libertarianism, is that it assumes anyone that violates your rights can be forced to pay retribution when they get caught. Unfortunately, this is hardly the case. For example, Bernard Maddoff will never be able to repay the billions of dollars he stole from investors. Better government oversight, could have limited the damages he caused.

Back in the late '90s Clinton, and the republican house retracted some government restrictions on banks, allowing them to take on riskier investments as part of their investment portfolios. Most Libertarians at the time thought this was a great idea, as it conformed with their beliefs that government should not interfere with business operations. Let a free market sort things out.

In retrospect, this turned out to be a huge mistake, and was partly responsible for the real estate collapse, and banking bailout that followed years later. Banks began treating real estate loans like cash in the bank. Smart, unethical individuals started financing overpriced homes to individuals that had no way of paying off the loans. These smart people got their commission for making the loan, and would transfer the loan as though it was cash to the banks. The loans were defaulted on, and the banks got stuck with a bunch of real estate that they would have to sell to recoup their cash. There were people at all levels of these organisations that knew what was going on. They played the game to maximize personal profit, and left everyone else holding the bag. There was no way to punish the culprits, even if they could be found. Throwing them in jail, maybe, but the money was gone.

Another problem with Ayn Rand libertarianism, is that it promotes privatizing almost everything. Thus we now have many privately run prisons. Anyone that runs a prison privately is going to want to maximize profits. The easiest way to maximize profits is to put more people in prison. Thus we have this segment of society that actually lobbies for putting people in prison. That's just not right.

I don't know a lot about Rand Paul, but I doubt he is a true libertarian, that blindly follows the Ayn Rand formula presented to us in her books.

Libertarianism sounded great when I was in college. It was like a mathematical formula to success. It's simplicity is what drew me in.

As a huge supporter of his father, my main argument against Rand is his flip-flopping. Ron never sold out on his principles, which is a big reason why he appealed to liberty-loving Americans like me. Rand, meanwhile, has changed his views on plenty of issues, including foreign aid, immigration, and Iran, in a vain attempt to suck up to the neocon establishment. I honestly think he's another Reagan or Obama: full of slick rhetoric, but will just be another big-government statist if elected. He can't be trusted.

To tack onto that, there were his comments about private companies being allowed to turn people away for service based on race, which he moved away from when it looked like the political fallout was going to overtake his campaign. It's the one problem I have with certain aspects of libertarian thinking. People are not perfectly neutral actors; we can pretty much all be dicks and buying influence is quite easy. And the free market correction of abuse does not seem like it could be a thing at a certain scale.

It's all about rolling back two things: The U.S. military machine and the Federal Reserve. He seems the only candidate even willing to discuss these issues. However, I'm not crazy about him signing onto that letter to Iran and a few other bonehead stunts he's pulled. I'll wait to see who the Libertarians put up.

Look, Rand Paul is not viable, for many reasons. I like some of his positions and in many ways I am glad he is in the Senate (I am a Dem from OH), but he has major failings and weaknesses which are quite damaging.

  1. He says really, really goofy things consistently, which makes him pretty much unelectable. He has shown to have some political instincts like his filibuster on drones and on government spying, but at other times has indicated a seriously lack of political sense.

  2. Libertarianism isn't even a real political philosophy, and cannot separate itself from the republican party. One good thing though is that he is pretty consistently against the idea of more war.

I kind of doubt that Rand has a lot of personal conviction about abortion, but we all know he can't come out as pro-choice while remaining in the republican party.

  1. Maybe the most devastating of his problems is that his wing of the party is small to start with, and doesn't tend to have a lot of power within the party.
